name: crumsort
workload: In-memory sort of 100,000-element arrays of 32/64/128-bit primitive types (int/long/long double) in random order, 100 samples, via the author's wolfsort benchmark harness (bench.c)
claimed_speedup: 64-bit ints: pdqsort avg 0.002668s vs crumsort avg 0.001927s, ~1.4x faster (derived from page data); 32-bit ints show a similar edge; on 128-bit long doubles pdqsort is faster than crumsort (crumsort is explicitly documented as slower there because of its partitioning scheme)
compiler_and_flags: g++ -O3 -w -fpermissive bench.c, on WSL gcc version 7.5.0 (Ubuntu 7.5.0-3ubuntu1~18.04)
tradeoffs: unstable, in-place, qsort()-compatible C API; branchless median/partition optimizations mainly benefit primitive integer types, not large value types (long double); porting guidance points to the simpler fluxsort/piposort instead
caveats: No CPU model is stated for the benchmark (only 'WSL gcc version...'), so it falls short of tier A; the README never benchmarks against std::sort/std::stable_sort directly, only against pdqsort and fluxsort (both already-catalogued projects), so baseline is recorded as pdqsort with baseline_in_list=false; numbers are from a 2024 README and result is type-dependent (crumsort loses to pdqsort on 128-bit types); The Unlicense is a public-domain dedication with no explicit patent grant
found_via: Blogs/talks: found via the 'Porting'/'Variants' cross-links in the already-known scandum/fluxsort and scandum/quadsort repos (surfaced from seed query "sorting algorithm faster than std::sort talk benchmark"); opened via gh api repos/scandum/crumsort and its README

name: blitsort
workload: In-memory stable sort of 100,000-element 32/64/128-bit arrays across many distributions (random order, random % 100, ascending, descending, sawtooth, random tail/half, etc.), 100 samples, via the author's wolfsort benchmark harness; README explicitly states 'Stablesort is g++'s std:stable_sort function'
claimed_speedup: random order, 64-bit: std::stable_sort avg 0.006207s vs blitsort avg 0.002518s, ~2.5x faster (derived from page data); random order, 32-bit: 0.006025s vs 0.002341s, ~2.6x faster (derived); much larger gaps on structured distributions (e.g. descending order: 0.000921s vs 0.000055s, ~17x, derived)
compiler_and_flags: g++ -O3 -w -fpermissive bench.c, on WSL 2 gcc version 7.5.0 (Ubuntu 7.5.0-3ubuntu1~18.04)
tradeoffs: stable, in-place (uses rotations instead of an O(n) swap buffer), qsort()-compatible C interface rather than a template/iterator-based API; also benchmarked against gfx::cpp-TimSort in the same table, where blitsort is faster in most but not all distributions
caveats: No CPU model is stated (only WSL/gcc version), and the run is inside WSL rather than bare metal, so this falls short of tier A methodology; numbers are from a 2024 README so may not reflect the current libstdc++ or current blitsort code; the largest speedups occur on already-ordered/patterned data rather than pure random data, which is a favorable case for adaptive sorts
found_via: Blogs/talks: found via cross-links from scandum/crumsort's 'Big O' comparison table and the wolfsort shootout referenced there (seed query "sorting algorithm faster than std::sort talk benchmark"); opened via gh api repos/scandum/blitsort and its README

name: gridsort
workload: In-memory stable sort of 1,000,000-element 32/64/128-bit arrays across multiple distributions (random order, ascending, descending, generic order, sawtooth, random tail/half, ascending tiles), 10 samples, via the author's wolfsort benchmark harness; a second, separate benchmark compares gridsort against the C library qsort() (a mergesort variant) at 100,000 elements
claimed_speedup: random order, 32-bit, 1M elements: std::stable_sort avg 0.073191s vs gridsort avg 0.051147s, ~1.4x faster (derived from page data); 'generic order' distribution: 0.041741s vs 0.016224s, ~2.6x faster (derived); against libc qsort() at 100,000 128-bit elements: 0.019996s vs 0.012730s, ~1.6x faster (derived)
compiler_and_flags: g++ -O3 -w -fpermissive bench.c (stdsort comparison), on WSL gcc version 7.5.0 (Ubuntu 7.5.0-3ubuntu1~18.04)
tradeoffs: stable comparison sort that stores data in an O(n) auxiliary 2-D self-balancing grid rather than sorting in-place; qsort()-compatible C interface; author states it 'was the fastest comparison sort for random data for a brief period' implying it has since been superseded on raw random-data speed by the author's own crumsort/fluxsort
caveats: No CPU model stated for either benchmark (WSL/gcc version only), so falls short of tier A; numbers are from a 2024 README; the qsort() comparison is against glibc's mergesort-based qsort, not std::sort, and is a separate, older benchmark image/table from the std::stable_sort one
found_via: Blogs/talks: found via cross-links from scandum/crumsort's 'Big O' comparison table and the wolfsort shootout (seed query "sorting algorithm faster than std::sort talk benchmark"); opened via gh api repos/scandum/gridsort and its README

name: voracious_radix_sort
workload: In-memory sort of i64 (and other primitive-type) arrays at sizes from 100 to 1000+ elements across ~25 synthetic distributions (uniform, +-1e9 range, ascending/descending +variants, Zipf, normal, sqrt, pipe organ, etc.), 5 iterations, single- and multi-threaded, run on the maintainer's own machine and checked into the repo's results/ directory
claimed_speedup: i64, 1000 elements, uniform distribution: Rust Std (stable sort) avg 36.525us vs Voracious (unstable/stable trait) avg 23.334us, ~1.56x faster (derived from page data); README states it is 'way faster than Rust standard sort and Rust unstable sort... on most types and data distributions', with radix sort's advantage expected to grow on the larger arrays it targets
compiler_and_flags: rustc ~1.46.0 stable (per README's 'Version' section); exact build flags for this specific benchmark run not stated
tradeoffs: out-of-place variants use up to 2x memory; only sorts primitive types and custom structs (no String/Tuple/Array support); radix sort is only worthwhile on larger arrays, falling back to native Rust sort for small inputs; best performance requires per-CPU tuning constants ('profiling'), and the shipped defaults are calibrated for the author's own Ryzen 3950x machine, so gains may not transfer to other CPUs
caveats: This compares against Rust's own std::sort/sort_unstable, not C++ std::sort directly, so compared_against_cpp_std_directly=false and baseline_stdlib is empty; the project's own benchmark methodology doesn't state optimization flags for this run, capping it at tier C; the quoted 1.56x figure is for a small (1000-element) array, which is below the size where radix sort is expected to shine according to the project's own docs
found_via: Blogs/talks: gh search repos "radix sort" language:rust --sort stars (variation on seed query "sorting algorithm faster than std::sort talk benchmark", adapted per 'Non-C++ implementations are welcome' rule); opened via gh api repos/lakwet/voracious_sort, its README, PROFILING.md, and results/benchmark_1_2_0/
